The twice-differentiable functions \(f\) and \(g\) are defined for all real numbers \(x\). Values of \(f, f^{\prime}, g\), and \(g^{\prime}\) for various values of \(x\) are given in the table above.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Find the \(x\)-coordinate of each relative minimum of \(f\) on the interval [-2,3]. Justify your answers.
\item[(b)] Explain why there must be a value \(c\), for \(-1<c<1\), such that \(f^{\prime \prime}(c)=0\).
\item[(c)] The function \(h\) is defined by \(h(x)=\ln (f(x))\). Find \(h^{\prime}(3)\). Show the computations that lead to your answer.
\item[(d)] Evaluate \(\int_{-2}^{3} f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x) d x\).
\item[(a)] \(x=1\) is the only critical point at which \(f^{\prime}\) changes sign from negative to positive. Therefore, \(f\) has a relative minimum at \(x=1\).
\item[(b)] \(f^{\prime}\) is differentiable \(\Rightarrow f^{\prime}\) is continuous on the interval \(-1 \leq x \leq 1\)
\[
\frac{f^{\prime}(1)-f^{\prime}(-1)}{1-(-1)}=\frac{0-0}{2}=0
\]
Therefore, by the Mean Value Theorem, there is at least one value \(c,-1<c<1\), such that \(f^{\prime \prime}(c)=0\).
\item[(c)] \(h^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{f(x)} \cdot f^{\prime}(x)\)
\[
h^{\prime}(3)=\frac{1}{f(3)} \cdot f^{\prime}(3)=\frac{1}{7} \cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{14}
\]
\item[(d)]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-2}^{3} f^{\prime}(g(x)) g^{\prime}(x) d x & =[f(g(x))]_{x=-2}^{x=3} \\
& =f(g(3))-f(g(-2)) \\
& =f(1)-f(-1) \\
& =2-8=-6
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{itemize}
